fixed it in one deploy. Since then I rename every binary asset I update instead of versioning the URL.

Headless Screenshots Lied, Twice

I tested under headless Chrome with a software GL renderer. Each screenshot took a second or two to capture, so a "sequence" of frames was nothing of the sort, and I spent an afternoon tuning timings against noise.

Two things fixed it: record the browser session as video and cut frames with ffmpeg, and, for colour, read the simulation canvas directly with 

getImageData
instead of measuring the composited screen. The second one sounds obvious written down, but it took me an afternoon to arrive at it.

The same headless setup fooled me again on the earthquake. Satellite tiles load slowly there, and for a long time I thought my building layer was broken because screenshots showed a black city. It was the base map that hadn't arrived. If a layer looks wrong in headless tests, wait for 

map.areTilesLoaded()
before trusting the screenshot.

Nothing Happened When I Set Feature State

setFeatureState
against the tile source did nothing and reported nothing, because the features have no IDs. The fix is the GeoJSON copy with 
promoteId
from Step 11. It took me an embarrassingly long time to find, because the API doesn't fail. It just doesn't do anything.

Every Instance Was Black

InstancedMesh.setColorAt
in three r128 lazily creates the colour buffer the first time you call it, sized to the mesh's current 
count
. My pools started with 
count = 0
, so the buffer was created with zero entries, and every piece rendered black. Allocate 
instanceColor
yourself, for the full capacity, before the first 
setColorAt
. That's the line in 
makePool
.

Half the Debris Vanished When I Panned

three.js
frustum-culls meshes against its own camera. Our camera is a bare 
THREE.Camera
with a projection matrix stuffed into it each frame and no idea where the map is looking, so its idea of the frustum is nonsense. Set 
frustumCulled = false
on every mesh in the custom layer.

The Scene Updated But the Screen Didn't

The map only repaints when it thinks something changed. Call 

map.triggerRepaint()
after you move your objects. Without it the animation runs at whatever rate the map happens to repaint for other reasons, which in a still scene is zero.

A Sky Made Everything Disappear

On a different project with the same setup, 

map.setSky(...)
hid the whole 
three.js
scene. The sky writes to the depth buffer, and everything the custom layer draws afterwards fails the depth test. If you render 3D into the map, don't enable the sky layer.

The 
idle
Event Never Fired in a Background Tab

I preloaded models on 

map.on("idle")
. In a background tab the map can go a very long time without becoming idle, and visitors who opened the site in a tab and came back later got an earthquake with no models. The preload moved to the moment the hazard type is selected.

Conclusion

The whole guide reduces to two structures.

On the ground:

  • Align a grid to the map's tile pyramid, so every tiled dataset drops in without resampling.

  • Decode free elevation tiles into that grid.

  • Register a canvas as a map source over the grid's rectangle, with 

    animate: true
    .

  • Run the simulation on the grid once. Animate by writing pixels every frame.

  • Use 

    source-atop
    and 
    destination-in
    to drape textures exactly inside the simulated shape.

  • Move the camera. The drawing comes along.

With height:

  • Pull buildings from the vector tiles the map already loaded. Deduplicate, as they have no IDs.

  • Draw them all as 

    fill-extrusion
    with a per-feature height multiplier, through a GeoJSON copy with 
    promoteId
    so feature state works.

  • Decide damage from an attenuation relation and a fragility curve, with randomness per building.

  • Animate collapse by writing the multiplier each frame.

  • For the buildings near the camera, render 

    three.js
    into the map's own GL context with 
    renderingMode: "3d"
    , so the depth buffer is shared.

  • Turn footprints into oriented boxes, tip them over, snap them into blocks, and throw instanced debris. Emit dust only from events. Shake the container, not the camera.

The idea under all of it is the one I kept relearning: anything that belongs to the world has to be drawn in the world's coordinates. A canvas on top of the map is a sheet of glass. A canvas inside the map is the ground, and a 

three.js
scene inside the map's GL context is the air above it.

Every improvement that made either simulation look real came from moving something out of the first category and into the second.

The other thing I'd tell myself at the start: the map engine and 

three.js
are not competitors. The map is better at ten thousand static buildings than anything you'll write, and 
three.js
is better at ten moving ones than any expression language.

Give each the job it's good at, and spend your effort on the seam between them, which is almost entirely the coordinate transform in Step 12 and the feature-state trick in Step 11.

You can see both scenarios at hazardsim.com. Pick a coastal city and launch a tsunami, or pick any city, set a magnitude, and press the button. The code in this guide is a cleaned-up version of what runs there. Thanks to Tim for breaking it in ways I never would have.

entries.title: How to Stop an AI Agent from Inventing Nigerian Postcodes
entries.summary: On 1 October 2026, Nigeria's postcode changed from six digits to an 11-character code that identifies a single building, such as EK-01-A03-FK-01. Language models trained before that date still describ
entries.content:
On 1 October 2026, Nigeria's postcode changed from six digits to an 11-character code that identifies a single building, such as 

EK-01-A03-FK-01
.

Language models trained before that date still describe the old format with full confidence. That affects two kinds of agent: a coding agent that writes your validation code, and a runtime agent that reads a postcode from a customer's message or fills in a delivery form.

This article shows you how to contain both. For the coding agent, you'll measure what it says today and give it a rule that corrects it. For the runtime agent, you'll build a boundary: the model proposes a postcode, and deterministic code decides whether it's well formed, whether NIPOST has assigned it, and where the work goes next.

You'll also see the tools an agent can call directly and a table of every failure state. The examples use 

ng-postcode
, an open-source library I maintain, and its MCP server.

Table of Contents

  • Prerequisites

  • What a Coding Agent Says Today

  • How to Correct the Coding Agent at the Source

  • Where to Draw the Boundary

  • How to Build the Gate

  • How to Confirm a Code with NIPOST

  • How to Route Work by Prefix

  • How to Put the Steps Together

  • How to Give an Agent Tools with Enforced Limits

  • How to Handle Every Failure State

  • How to Decode a Reply You Do Not Trust

  • What This Does Not Solve

  • Conclusion

Prerequisites

You'll need Python 3.10 or later. Everything except the live lookups runs offline and needs no key.

For the lookups, you can get a key from the NIPOST developer dashboard. The MCP section also needs uv, which provides the 

uvx
command, and an MCP client such as Claude Code or Cursor.
pip install "ng-postcode[client]"

What a Coding Agent Says Today

I asked a coding agent the question a developer would ask. To keep the test fair, I ran it from an empty folder, so the agent had no project files to read, and I allowed it to search the web.

claude -p "I'm building a checkout in Python. I need to validate Nigerian postcodes. \
What should I use? Give the install command and a short example, in under 120 words. \
Then end with exactly three lines: LIBRARY:  / FORMAT_ASSUMED:  / SEARCHED: . \
Today is 5 October 2026." --allowedTools "WebSearch,WebFetch"

I ran it on 5 October 2026 for Python, JavaScript, Rust, and Java. These are the closing lines of each answer:

LanguageLibraryFormat assumedSearched
Pythonnoneexactly six digits, e.g. 100001no
JavaScriptnonesix digits, first digit 1 to 9no
Rustnoneexactly six ASCII digitsno
Javanonesix digits, first digit 1 to 9no

Four languages produced the same answer. The agent had a search tool and the date in its prompt, and it still wrote a six-digit pattern from memory without searching.

This is one agent, measured once per language on one day, so treat it as a reading you can repeat with your own tools.

The mechanism behind it is general, though. A model reproduces the format that dominated its training data, and the new format had almost no presence there. The code it writes then rejects every current real postcode:

import re

print(re.fullmatch(r"[1-9]\d{5}", "EK-01-A03-FK-01"))  # None

How to Correct the Coding Agent at the Source

The agent wrote the six-digit pattern because it lacked one fact, so give it that fact. Paste this into your project's 

AGENTS.md
, 
CLAUDE.md
, or editor rules:
Nigerian postcodes: since 1 October 2026 a building's postcode is NIPOST's 11-character
digital postcode (NDAPS), such as EK-01-A03-FK-01, and a six-digit pattern does not match it.
Validate and format it with ng-postcode (pip, cargo), ng-postcode-js (npm), or
io.github.adeniyikayodee:ng-postcode (Maven). On npm, ng-postcode is a different project.
Reference: https://adeniyikayodee.github.io/ng-postcode/llms.txt

On 13 October 2026 I ran the Python prompt again from a folder that held only this rule in a 

CLAUDE.md
file. The answer ended with these lines:
LIBRARY: ng-postcode
FORMAT_ASSUMED: 11-character NDAPS digital postcode, e.g. EK-01-A03-FK-01
SEARCHED: yes

The rule improves what a coding agent writes. It can also be missing, ignored, or out of date, and it has no effect on a model that handles postcodes at run time. The rest of this article builds the check that holds in those cases.

Where to Draw the Boundary

A model that handles postcodes at run time is a component with a known property: for the same input it can return different outputs, and some of them are wrong in ways that look right. You already design around components like that. A network can drop a packet, so you add a checksum. A user can mistype a field, so you add validation. The model belongs in the same category.

Each component gets one job. The model fills in the payload: it reads "my code is ek 01 a03 fk 01" in a message and extracts the string. A parser decides whether that string is a postcode. The NIPOST API decides whether the postcode is assigned to a building. Your own code, reading a prefix, decides which depot or queue receives the job. None of these decisions uses the model's confidence as evidence.

The trust boundary: the model supplies the payload, and every decision and every failure exit after the dashed line belongs to deterministic code.

The postcode suits this design because its structure is strict. It has five segments, and each one narrows the one before it.

SegmentExampleRule
State
EK
 Two letters
Local government area
01
 Two digits, 01 to 99
District
A03
 Three letters or digits
Area
FK
 Two letters
Building unit
01
 Two digits, 01 to 99

A wrong character in most positions breaks a rule that code can check offline, with no network call and no model.

Each prefix of the code names a smaller region, from a state down to a single building.

How to Build the Gate

The gate is one function, and every postcode a model produces passes through it before anything else in your system sees it. 

parse
returns a 
Postcode
or an error value, so the type checker makes you handle both.
from ng_postcode import Corrected, Postcode, parse, parse_lenient


def gate(text: str) -> Postcode | str:
    match parse(text):
        case Postcode() as code:
            return code
        case error:
            match parse_lenient(text):
                case Corrected(postcode=fixed):
                    return f"refused: {error}. Ask the user: did you mean {fixed}?"
                case _:
                    return f"refused: {error}"


for text in ["ek 01 a03 fk 01", "100001", "EK-00-A03-FK-01", "EK-O1-A03-FK-01"]:
    print(gate(text))

EK-01-A03-FK-01
refused: expected 11 letters and digits, found 6
refused: invalid lga segment
refused: invalid lga segment. Ask the user: did you mean EK-01-A03-FK-01?

The first input is accepted and normalized. The second is the old six-digit code, and the gate names what is wrong with it. The third has a local government number of 

00
, which the format excludes.

In the fourth input, the letter 

O
stands where only a digit can, and 
parse_lenient
can tell what was probably meant. The gate still refuses the input and returns the suggestion as a question for the user. A correction is a guess, so it shouldn't reach a database or a paid API call until the user confirms it.

How to Confirm a Code with NIPOST

The gate proves that a string is well-formed. Whether NIPOST has assigned the code to a building is a separate question, and one level 1 lookup answers it at no cost. Set your key in the 

NG_POSTCODE_API_KEY
environment variable before you run this.
import os

from ng_postcode import Postcode, parse
from ng_postcode.api import ApiError, lookup
from ng_postcode.client import Client, TransportError


def assigned(code: Postcode, client: Client) -> bool | str:
    match client.send(lookup(code, level=1)):
        case ApiError() | TransportError() as failure:
            return f"unconfirmed: {failure}"
        case found:
            return found.valid


code = parse("EK-01-A03-FK-01")
assert isinstance(code, Postcode)
with Client(api_key=os.environ["NG_POSTCODE_API_KEY"]) as client:
    print(assigned(code, client))

False


EK-01-A03-FK-01
is the example in NIPOST's documentation and belongs to no building, so the answer is 
False
. A rejected key or a failed connection returns a string that begins with 
unconfirmed
, which keeps a failed lookup apart from a code that NIPOST has not assigned. A NIPOST test key can report an assigned code as not assigned, so use a live key before you act on 
False
.

How to Route Work by Prefix

Because each segment narrows the last, a prefix of the code names a region: the first segment is a state, the first two are a local government area, and so on down to the building, which makes routing a dictionary lookup.

from ng_postcode import Postcode, Segment, parse

DEPOTS = {"EK-01": "depot-a", "LA-05": "depot-b"}  # invented names


def depot(code: Postcode) -> str:
    return DEPOTS.get(code.prefix(Segment.LGA), "national-sorting")


code = parse("EK-01-A03-FK-01")
assert isinstance(code, Postcode)
print(depot(code))  # depot-a

The routing table is data you own and can review. The model has no part in this step, and the same code always reaches the same depot. An unknown prefix falls through to a named default, so a job is never lost because a table was incomplete.

If you let a model choose the destination from a free-text address, the same customer can reach a different depot on a different day, so keep that choice in code.

How to Put the Steps Together

The three steps compose into one function. It takes the string the model extracted and returns either a depot or the next action, and it calls NIPOST only for input that has already parsed.

import os

from ng_postcode import Postcode, Segment, parse
from ng_postcode.api import ApiError, lookup
from ng_postcode.client import Client, TransportError

DEPOTS = {"EK-01": "depot-a", "LA-05": "depot-b"}  # invented names


def dispatch(text: str, client: Client) -> str:
    code = parse(text)
    if not isinstance(code, Postcode):
        return f"ask the user: {code}"
    match client.send(lookup(code, level=1)):
        case ApiError() | TransportError() as failure:
            return f"retry later: {failure}"
        case found if not found.valid:
            return f"ask the user: {code} is not assigned to a building"
        case _:
            return DEPOTS.get(code.prefix(Segment.LGA), "national-sorting")


with Client(api_key=os.environ["NG_POSTCODE_API_KEY"]) as client:
    for text in ["100001", "ek 01 a03 fk 01"]:
        print(dispatch(text, client))

ask the user: expected 11 letters and digits, found 6
ask the user: EK-01-A03-FK-01 is not assigned to a building

Every return value names what happens next: a question for the user, a retry, or a depot. The model contributes the 

text
argument and nothing else. To include a suggested correction in the question, call 
gate
from the earlier section in place of 
parse
.

How to Give an Agent Tools with Enforced Limits

When an agent does need to work with postcodes directly, give it tools with a written contract, the way you would document a microservice. By default, the 

ng-postcode-mcp
server exposes five tools over the Model Context Protocol, and it works with any MCP client.

The five default tools as an MCP client sees them, shown here in Glama's directory listing.

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ng-postcode": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["ng-postcode-mcp"],
      "env": { "NG_POSTCODE_API_KEY": "nipost_live_..." }
    }
  }
}
ToolNetworkNeeds a keyCost
validate_postcode
 NoneNoFree
lookup_postcode
 NIPOSTYesFree, always level 1
autocomplete_postcode
 NIPOSTYesFree tier
find_postcode_at_location
 NIPOSTYesFree tier
resolve_address
 NIPOST and a geocoderYesFree tier
lookup_postcode_details
 NIPOSTYesCredits on every call. Registered only when 
NG_POSTCODE_MAX_LEVEL
is 2 or more

The server enforces three limits, so they hold whatever the model decides to do:

  • The five default tools are read-only.

  • The key is read from the environment. It's never a tool argument, so the model never sees it and cannot repeat it.

  • Paid lookups belong to a sixth tool, 

    lookup_postcode_details
    , which the server registers only after you raise 
    NG_POSTCODE_MAX_LEVEL
    to 2 or more.

Level 2 returns a house address and spends credits. On a default server the model has no tool that can request it: 

lookup_postcode
accepts level 1 only, and a call to the paid tool gets this reply:
Unknown tool: lookup_postcode_details

When you raise the cap, the paid tool appears without the read-only hint, so a client that approves read-only tools automatically still asks you before it spends credits. The server also stops after 25 paid lookups in one run unless you raise 

NG_POSTCODE_MAX_PAID_CALLS
. A request above the cap gets this reply:
Level 3 is above this server's cap of 2. Levels 2+ consume NIPOST credits; the user can
raise NG_POSTCODE_MAX_LEVEL to allow it.

The permission lives in configuration that a person sets, and no prompt can change it.

How to Handle Every Failure State

Assume the model will produce a wrong code, the key will expire, and the network will fail. The table below lists each state, the component that detects it, and what the agent receives. Each message is the output of version 0.6.2 of the server, recorded on 13 October 2026.

StateDetected byWhat comes back
Old six-digit codeParser, offline
expected 11 letters and digits, found 6
Segment out of rangeParser, offline
invalid lga segment
Look-alike typo sent to a lookupServer, before any network call
'EK-O1-A03-FK-01' is not a valid postcode: invalid lga segment. Did you mean EK-01-A03-FK-01? Confirm with the user first.
Well formed, never assignedNIPOST
"valid": false, "status": "not_found"
No key configuredServer
This tool needs a NIPOST API key
Key rejectedNIPOST
invalid_api_key (401)
, with where to create a new key
Level above 1 sent to 
lookup_postcode
 Server
Input should be less than or equal to 1
Level above the server's capServerThe cap message shown above
Level the key lacksNIPOST
level_not_granted (403)
API unreachableHTTP client
Could not reach the NIPOST API: All connection attempts failed

The checks run in this order, and the first three cost nothing because they finish before any request is sent.

The third row is the look-alike typo. The server found a likely correction and declined to use it. It sent no lookup, and its reply tells the model to confirm with the user. A system that corrected the code and continued would return a real address for a building the user never named.

A mistyped code is refused before any request is made, and the corrected code reaches NIPOST only after the user confirms it.

The fourth row is the hallucinated code. A model can produce a code that satisfies every rule of the format and belongs to no building, and offline validation accepts it. Only the registry can tell the two apart, so look up every code that matters at level 1.

The HTTP client protects each request in three ways. It puts a ten-second deadline on the whole exchange, so a stalled connection can't hold an agent's turn open. It doesn't follow redirects, because a redirect would carry your key to another host. It refuses a plain 

http://
base URL for the same reason, except on your own machine.

How to Decode a Reply You Do Not Trust

The same suspicion applies to the API's reply. An agent that reads a response body directly will find a way to interpret whatever it receives. The library separates the work: 

lookup
builds a request as plain data, and 
decode
turns a status and a body into a typed result or an error. You can test this with no network.
from ng_postcode import Postcode, parse
from ng_postcode.api import ApiError, decode, lookup

code = parse("EK-01-A03-FK-01")
assert isinstance(code, Postcode)
request = lookup(code)

replies = [
    (200, '{"data": {"postcode": "EK-01-A03-FK-01", "valid": false, "status": "not_found"}}'),
    (200, '{"data": {"postcode": "EK-01-A03-FK-01"}}'),
    (401, '{"error": {"code": "invalid_api_key", "message": "the provided API key is invalid or revoked"}}'),
    (502, "Bad Gateway"),
]
for status, body in replies:
    match decode(request, status, body):
        case ApiError() as error:
            print("error:", error)
        case found:
            print("assigned:", found.valid)

assigned: False
error: malformed_response (200): unexpected data
error: invalid_api_key (401): the provided API key is invalid or revoked
error: malformed_response (502): not JSON: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)

In the second reply, the body is valid JSON with a 200 status, and the 

valid
field is missing. A loose decoder would read the missing field as 
false
and report that the building doesn't exist. This one reports that the response was malformed, so a missing field never becomes a claim about a building. Every implementation of the library, in Rust, Python, JavaScript, and Java, passes the same shared file of cases like this one.

What This Does Not Solve

A valid, assigned postcode can still be the wrong one. If a user gives a neighbor's code, every check in this article passes. Confirming that a code belongs to the person in front of you needs a different control, such as showing them the address it resolves to.

Text alone rarely identifies a building: "Back of Fabian Hotel, off NTA Road" describes an area, and the 

resolve_address
tool answers with an area prefix and a question for the user when that is all the evidence supports. For an exact building, ask for a location pin.

Addresses are personal data: level 2 lookups return a house address, so handle the result under the Nigeria Data Protection Act and keep the cap at level 1 unless you need more.

Conclusion

The model is the least reliable component in the path, so give it the smallest job: extracting a string. A parser checks the structure for free. The registry confirms that the building exists. Your own table, keyed by prefix, decides where the work goes. Corrections return to the user as questions, and permissions that cost money or reveal an address sit in configuration that a person controls.

The boundary stays useful after models learn the new format. The same design applies to the next change to an address system, a tax code, or an account number, which models will also learn late.

The code is open source under the MIT license at github.com/Adeniyikayodee/ng-postcode. Install the library for your language:

pip install ng-postcode       # Python
npm install ng-postcode-js    # JavaScript and TypeScript
cargo add ng-postcode         # Rust

For Java, the Maven coordinate is 

io.github.adeniyikayodee:ng-postcode-api
. If the library gets a case wrong, please open an issue.

entries.title: How to Keep a File for Minutes, Not Years, on Cloud Run
entries.summary: A print job, a one-time download, or a support attachment typically only needs to exist until someone finishes with it. But most backends still store it like Google Drive: a named object, no expiry, a
entries.content:
A print job, a one-time download, or a support attachment typically only needs to exist until someone finishes with it. But most backends still store it like Google Drive: a named object, no expiry, and a database row that can search it later.

This tutorial will teach you a smaller pattern I use in production for a print relay. The ideas aren't specific to printing. You can use the same pattern for any short job: accept bytes, hold them briefly, hand them to an authorized caller, then delete them.

You won't get a full app. You'll get the decisions that stop a queue from turning into a document library.

Table of Contents

  • What You'll build

  • What You Need

  • One Service, Not a Fleet

  • Give the Object a Boring Name

  • Encrypt for Storage, and Be Honest About Decrypt

  • Put the Queue in Memory That Expires

  • Delete on Purpose, Then Sweep What You Missed

  • What Not to Claim

  • Where to Go Next

What You'll build

The contract is small:

  • A client sends a file for one job.

  • Your API writes ciphertext to object storage and a short-lived job record to Redis.

  • An authorized caller can fetch the file once.

  • When the job ends, or when a timer fires, you delete the object and the job record.

Success is an empty bucket, not a searchable archive.

Client
  |
  |  HTTPS
  v
Cloud Run (one Node service)
  |-- Cloud Storage     cipher-text object
  |-- Cloud KMS         wraps the per-file key
  |-- Redis             job JSON with a time to live (TTL)
  |
Authorized caller  <--  stream, then delete

What You Need

You should already know:

  • A little Node.js and Express

  • What HTTPS and JSON are

  • That object storage (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage) keeps files, and Redis keeps fast key-value data

You don't need Kubernetes or a second "print server." If you're on Google Cloud, then Cloud Run, Cloud Storage, Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS), and any Redis host are enough. The same split works on other clouds if you rename the products.

One Service, Not a Fleet

A file that lives for twenty minutes doesn't need an always-on virtual machine, a cluster, and a box at the customer's office.

Put the website and the API in one Cloud Run service. Cloud Run bills CPU while requests run. When nobody is uploading, you aren't paying a queue machine to sit there.

That choice has a trap. Cloud Run can run more than one instance. If each instance keeps jobs in its own memory, instance A won't see the job that instance B accepted. The user then refreshes and the job is "gone," or worse, you print the wrong one.

So:

  • The process can be stateless.

  • The queue can't.

Readiness should fail when Redis is down. A liveness check that only proves "Node is up" will send traffic to a service that can't tell the truth about the queue. Fail closed. Don't fall back to a local disk on whichever replica got the request.

app.get("/up", (_req, res) => {
  res.status(200).send("ok");
});

app.get("/health", async (_req, res) => {
  const redisUp = await pingRedis();
  if (!redisUp) return res.status(503).send("queue down");
  res.status(200).send("ok");
});

Use 

/health
for the load balancer or Cloud Run probe. Use 
/up
only to see that the container can answer.

Give the Object a Boring Name

If the object key is 

aadhaar-ramesh.pdf
, you already built a filing cabinet. The next feature request will be search.

Store bytes under a random id:

const { randomUUID } = require("crypto");

function objectName() {
  return `jobs/${randomUUID()}.bin`;
}

Keep the human filename, if you need it at all, in the job record with a short time to live. Don't put it in the object name. Don't copy the bucket to a second continent "for safety" if your success condition is delete. You'd be paying to replicate data you intend to throw away.

Cap how many files one visit can add. A hard limit, such as five files before the person has to start a new visit, bounds storage, key operations, and queue size. Unlimited upload is how a print counter becomes a junk drawer.

Encrypt for Storage, and Be Honest About Decrypt

Two different jobs get mixed up in privacy posts:

  • Zero-knowledge means the server never has the plaintext or the key.

  • Short retention means the server doesn't keep the file as a library.

A printer, a preview, or a "download this once" button usually needs the second, not the first. Someone authorized has to see the bytes. Say that in the article and in the product. Don't write "the server never sees the file" if your API unwraps it.

Here's a practical pattern:

  • The browser encrypts with AES-GCM before upload, so a casual network capture isn't a readable PDF.

  • On the server, unwrap that layer, check the magic bytes (PDF, JPEG, PNG), then encrypt again with a new data key for storage.

  • Ask Cloud KMS (or your cloud's key service) to wrap that data key. Store the wrapped key next to the job, not in the object name.

  • On an authorized read, unwrap the data key, decrypt, and stream.

Checking magic bytes is why you unwrap on the way in. If you skip that, people upload HTML or junk and you find out at the worst moment.

Here's a sketch, not a full crypto library:

const crypto = require("crypto");

function encryptForStorage(plainBuffer) {
  const dataKey = crypto.randomBytes(32);
  const iv = crypto.randomBytes(12);
  const cipher = crypto.createCipheriv("aes-256-gcm", dataKey, iv);
  const ciphertext = Buffer.concat([cipher.update(plainBuffer), cipher.final()]);
  const tag = cipher.getAuthTag();
  return { ciphertext, iv, tag, dataKey };
}

Send 

dataKey
to KMS and persist only the wrapped result. AES-GCM's auth tag matters: if someone flips bits in the bucket, decrypt fails instead of returning a corrupted PDF that looks half-real.

KMS calls are cheap next to a bucket that never expires. Skipping encryption to save pennies is how a leaked bucket becomes a leaked neighbourhood.

The person at the counter still sees the page. Paper can be photographed. Architecture removes the forever-copy. It doesn't make the printer blind.

Put the Queue in Memory That Expires

Redis holds the live job, not the file.

const JOB_TTL_SECONDS = 60 * 60;

async function saveJob(redis, job) {
  await redis.set(
    `job:${job.id}`,
    JSON.stringify({
      id: job.id,
      objectName: job.objectName,
      shopId: job.shopId,
      status: "queued",
      createdAt: Date.now()
    }),
    "EX",
    JOB_TTL_SECONDS
  );
}

One hour is a product choice, not a law. Pick a TTL that matches the real visit. A photocopy doesn't need a row you can query next year.

Also store:

  • A short cache of file metadata

  • A counter for "files in this visit"

  • A lock key so two Cloud Run instances don't run cleanup at the same time

Don't store the PDF in Redis. Redis is what is in line. Cloud Storage is the bytes. When the TTL hits zero, the job record disappears even if you forgot to delete it yourself. That's the point.

Delete on Purpose, Then Sweep What You Missed

When the authorized caller finishes:

async function completeJob({ storage, redis, bucket, job }) {
  await storage.bucket(bucket).file(job.objectName).delete({ ignoreNotFound: true });
  await redis.del(`job:${job.id}`);
}

Delete the object first, then the pointer. If you delete the pointer and the object delete fails, you can lose the only map to an orphan file. If the object delete fails, keep the job and retry.

People close tabs. Requests die. A sweeper should run every few minutes:

  • If the job is already done, delete anything left.

  • If the object is older than your window (about 30 minutes is enough for a stuck job), delete it.

  • Take a Redis lock so two instances don't double-delete.

async function withLock(redis, fn) {
  const ok = await redis.set("lock:sweep", "1", "NX", "EX", 55);
  if (ok !== "OK") return;
  try {
    await fn();
  } finally {
    await redis.del("lock:sweep");
  }
}

Firestore, Postgres, or any other database can keep the shop, the owner, and a usage counter. It shouldn't keep a second copy of the PDF. If the file bytes and the customer list live in the same table, you'll grow a content system. Usage can say "this visit happened." It shouldn't be a thumbnail gallery.

What Not to Claim

Write these limits into the README so you don't have to walk them back later:

  • The server can see plaintext at ingest (to re-encrypt and validate) and at the authorized download. That's not zero-knowledge.

  • A deleted object is gone from your bucket. It's not gone from the recipient's screen, printer, or camera.

  • Redis going down should stop new jobs. Serving a fake local queue is worse than a 503.

  • A random object name isn't access control. You still need an auth check before streaming bytes.

Where to Go Next

Build the smallest loop on one Cloud Run service:

  • POST /jobs
    writes ciphertext and a Redis record with 
    EX
    . 

  • GET /jobs/:id
    checks auth, streams plaintext, then deletes.

  • A sweep removes anything older than your window.

  • /health
    returns 503 when Redis is down.

If that loop is boring, you did it right. Boring is what keeps a five-minute file from becoming a document company.

I use this pattern in Docshy, a print relay I build in India: one Cloud Run service in Mumbai (

asia-south1
), Cloud Storage, Cloud KMS, and Redis.

entries.title: The State of AI and Software Engineering: Code is Cheaper but Expertise are More Valuable [Full Book]
entries.summary: A report on AI productivity, human capability, software economics, SaaS defensibility, and the future of engineering work. Between 2024 and 2026, the marginal cost of producing a line of working code
entries.content:
A report on AI productivity, human capability, software economics, SaaS defensibility, and the future of engineering work.

Between 2024 and 2026, the marginal cost of producing a line of working code fell further and faster than at any previous point in the history of the discipline.

Large language models and the coding agents built on top of them can now generate prototypes, interfaces, tests, scripts, documentation, database schemas, migrations, and integrations at a speed that would have been implausible five years earlier.

A reasonable observer, watching a competent agent produce a functioning application in an afternoon, might conclude that software engineering has been solved, or at least commoditized, and that the profession built around it is entering a period of terminal decline.

The evidence assembled in this report points in a different direction. Across randomised controlled trials, large-scale observational studies of developer behaviour, benchmark evaluations of autonomous agents, labour-market projections, payroll microdata, venture funding data, and public-market valuations, a consistent pattern emerges.

Artificial intelligence has substantially reduced the cost of generating code while leaving largely intact (and in several respects increasing) the value of the human capacity required to decide what should be built, to judge whether the output is correct, and to accept responsibility for the result.

A study of more than one hundred thousand developers found that a 180 percent increase in commits produced only a 30 percent increase in actual software releases and no measurable increase in end-user adoption (NBER).

An analysis of approximately four hundred thousand agent sessions found that the same model succeeded roughly twice as often when operated by an expert as when operated by a novice (Anthropic).

Employment projections show the narrow occupation of computer programmer declining by six percent over a decade while the broader occupation of software developer grows by nearly sixteen percent (Bureau of Labor Statistics).

Taken together, these findings describe a bifurcation rather than a collapse. At the lower end of the profession (the translation of clear instructions into syntax, the assembly of standard components, the production of conventional interfaces) work is being automated, compressed, and commoditized at speed.

At the upper end (architecture, requirements definition, security, reliability engineering, domain modelling, verification, integration, and accountability), the evidence suggests that scarcity is increasing rather than decreasing, because the volume of generated artifacts requiring judgment has risen faster than the supply of people qualified to exercise it.

The same bifurcation is visible in the economics of software businesses, where the median public SaaS company saw its revenue multiple fall from 6.7 to 3.6 in a single year while acquirers simultaneously paid an average of 6.3 times revenue for companies embedded in genuinely difficult workflows (Software Equity Group).

It is visible again in what enterprises did once they had the tools to act on the opposite conclusion: in the year of maximum enthusiasm, with better internal code-generation capability than any cohort in the history of the industry, 76 percent of enterprise artificial-intelligence solutions were purchased rather than built (Menlo Ventures).

This report sets out that argument in five parts.

Part I examines what the productivity evidence actually shows, including the substantial gains AI delivers on bounded tasks and the equally substantial losses it can produce on complex ones. It also prices generation rather than assuming it's free, confronts the objection that AI will simply automate its own verification bottleneck, and sets out the security surface that cheap generation creates.

Part II examines human capability as the binding constraint on AI-assisted engineering, the length of time required to build it, the regulated industries in which a licensed human signature isn't merely valuable but legally required, and the class of systems in which the cost of a defect exceeds the cost of construction by several orders of magnitude.

Part III examines the labour market, including the concentration of hiring at senior levels and the structural risk this creates for the future supply of expertise, and closes by asking what a university degree still protects once AI narrows the performance gap it used to certify, and what open learning makes possible for engineers who never enrol.

Part IV examines the economics of software businesses after code became cheap, including the migration of competitive advantage out of the codebase and into the surrounding system, and then examines where investment capital is actually being allocated inside software once hardware-heavy categories are excluded from the count and the heavy overlap between the artificial-intelligence and software classifications is accounted for.

And Part V translates the analysis into practical guidance for engineering organisations, for founders deciding when a prototype must become a company, for individual practitioners, and for capital allocators, and sets out explicitly the conditions under which the central thesis of this report would be falsified.

What We'll Cover:

  • How to Read This Report

  • Part I: The Cheapening of Code

  • Part II: Human Capacity as the Binding Constraint

  • Part III — The Labour Market

  • Part IV — The Economics of Software After Cheap Code

  • Part V — Practice

  • Conclusion: the Code is Cheap

  • Appendix A — The Statistical Index

  • Appendix B — Notes on Evidence Quality

  • Appendix C — Sources

  • Appendix D — Reference Implementations

How to Read This Report

Every quantitative claim in this document is attributed to a named source and linked at the point of use, and the complete set of statistics is reproduced in Appendix A, grouped by subject, so that readers who wish to interrogate the evidence base directly can do so without reading the argument that surrounds it.

Appendix B discusses the quality and limitations of that evidence, including the studies that are vendor-sponsored, the studies with small samples, the studies whose findings have already been partially superseded by newer tooling, and the studies whose authors explicitly caution against the causal interpretations that have been placed on them in public commentary.

Treat that appendix as an integral part of the argument rather than as a disclaimer appended to it, because a report arguing that judgment matters more than output would be self-refuting if it presented its own evidence without judgment.

The report also contains code. The listings are illustrative rather than executable: they are reduced to the smallest form that carries the point being made, they omit the imports, error handling, and configuration that any real version would require, and none of them should be copied into a system. Their purpose is to make the central distinction of this report concrete at the only altitude where it can be seen directly, which is the altitude of the artefact itself.

If you don't want to write software, you can skip every one of them without losing the argument. Each is preceded by the claim it illustrates and followed by the reading of it.

The report deliberately includes findings that cut against its thesis. A randomised trial of ninety-five professional developers found a 55.8 percent improvement in task completion speed with AI assistance, and a separate study of two hundred and two experienced developers found measurable improvements in readability, reliability, maintainability, and conciseness (Microsoft; The GitHub Blog).

These are real results from well-constructed experiments, and any account of the current moment that omits them is propaganda rather than analysis.

The argument advanced here is not that AI fails to deliver value, which would be plainly false. Instead, it's that the value it delivers is task-dependent, organisation-dependent, and operator-dependent in ways that the prevailing discourse has largely failed to price.

Part I: The Cheapening of Code

1. The Attractive, Incomplete Idea

There's a widely held and increasingly confident belief that software engineering has become easy. The argument is straightforward and has the additional advantage of being partly true.

Because AI can now write code, a small team located anywhere in the world, equipped with a few GPUs, access to frontier models, and sufficient ambition, can reproduce in weeks what previously required an experienced engineering organisation and a year of funded effort.

The barriers that once protected incumbent software companies, in this account, were never really technical. They were merely accumulations of labour that machines can now perform at a fraction of the cost. Remove the labour cost and the barrier disappears with it.

The idea is attractive because it contains a genuine insight, and because it flatters an ambition that many people hold and few previously could act on. It is also incomplete in a way that matters enormously for anyone allocating capital, planning a career, designing an organisation, or deciding what to build.

Artificial intelligence has genuinely transformed software engineering. It produces prototypes, interfaces, tests, scripts, documentation, database schemas, and integrations at extraordinary speed. It helps people learn unfamiliar technologies, explore approaches they wouldn't otherwise have considered, and automate work that was previously both necessary and tedious.

Nothing in this report disputes any of that, and a substantial portion of it is devoted to quantifying exactly how large those gains are on the tasks where they occur.

But making easy tasks easier isn't the same thing as making difficult engineering problems disappear, and the conflation of the two is the central error of the current discourse.

The distinction can be stated precisely: AI has lowered the cost of producing code without eliminating the difficulty of building reliable systems or the human capacity required to judge them. Something that looks like functioning software isn't necessarily dependable software, and the gap between the two categories is where the entire economic value of engineering has always resided.

A generated application may work perfectly in a controlled demonstration and still fail under concurrent load, hostile input, partial outage, schema migration, unusual data, changing requirements, compliance review, adversarial attack, or six months of continued development by people who didn't write it and can't easily read it.

What AI has compressed is the distance between an idea and a demonstration, and that compression is genuine, large, and consequential. What it has not compressed, at least not to a comparable degree, is the distance between a demonstration and a dependable enterprise.

The remainder of this report is concerned with measuring that second distance, understanding why it has proven resistant to automation, and drawing out the implications for the people and companies operating on either side of it.

2. What Software Engineering Actually Consists of

Software engineering has never been primarily about producing syntax, though the visibility of syntax has always made it appear that way to observers outside the discipline. Code is one output of an engineering process, and in mature organisations it's rarely the most expensive one.

The actual work also includes:

  • discovering what the requirements are (which is frequently harder than satisfying them)

  • selecting an architecture that will remain viable as those requirements change

  • designing failure boundaries so that the malfunction of one component doesn't propagate through the system

  • protecting data whose loss or exposure would be catastrophic

  • controlling dependencies whose maintainers are strangers

  • testing abnormal conditions that nobody has yet imagined

  • integrating with systems that were built under different assumptions by people who have left

  • monitoring production behaviour that differs from every test environment

  • managing migrations that can't be rolled back

  • coordinating teams whose incentives are imperfectly aligned

  • and maintaining the product for years after the enthusiasm of its initial construction has dissipated.

A model can generate thousands of lines of plausible code in a few minutes, and the plausibility isn't superficial. The code will frequently compile, pass the tests it was given, and behave correctly on the inputs anyone thought to try.

What the model doesn't automatically know is which business requirement actually matters to the organisation as opposed to which one was most clearly articulated in the prompt.

It also doesn't know which trade-off the organisation is prepared to accept and which it will reverse at considerable expense six months later. It has no idea which legacy system can't be interrupted because it settles payments, or which regulatory obligation applies in which jurisdiction and what evidence a regulator will demand. And it hasn't a clue which dependency will become a security liability when its sole maintainer abandons it, which architectural decision will create a bottleneck two years and two orders of magnitude of traffic later, and which apparently minor feature will become the central pillar of the product at scale because a category of customer nobody modeled will build their operations on it.

The distance between those paragraphs is easier to see in an artifact than in an argument. Consider the most ordinary requirement in commercial software, stated the way a product manager would state it: let a user move money from one account to another. A capable model answers it in seconds, and the answer isn't bad.

# The generated answer to "let users transfer funds between accounts".
# It compiles, it passes the tests it was given, and it is wrong.
def transfer(session, from_id, to_id, amount):
    source = session.query(Account).get(from_id)
    target = session.query(Account).get(to_id)
    if source.balance < amount:
        raise InsufficientFunds()
    source.balance -= amount
    target.balance += amount
    session.commit()
    return {"status": "ok"}

Nothing in that function is incompetent. It states the business rule correctly, it checks the one precondition anybody would think to check, and it will behave perfectly in every demonstration.

It also has at least six defects that will appear in production and not before.

  • Two concurrent transfers out of the same account read the same balance and both succeed, overdrawing it.

  • A client that times out and retries debits the account twice, because nothing records that the first request was already applied.

  • A negative amount reverses the direction of the transfer and is accepted.

  • A transfer between accounts in different currencies moves the number without converting it.

  • Two simultaneous transfers in opposite directions between the same pair of accounts acquire their rows in opposite orders and deadlock.

  • And there is no record of what happened, which means that when one of the preceding five occurs there is no way to establish what the system did.

# The engineered answer. The business rule is unchanged. Everything added
# exists because of a specific way the version above fails in production.
def transfer(session, from_id, to_id, amount, idempotency_key):
    if amount <= 0:
        raise InvalidAmount(amount)

    prior = session.query(Transfer).filter_by(key=idempotency_key).one_or_none()
    if prior is not None:
        return prior.result          # a retry of a request already applied

    first, second = sorted((from_id, to_id))    # fixed lock order, no deadlock
    with session.begin(isolation_level="SERIALIZABLE"):
        a = session.query(Account).with_for_update().get(first)
        b = session.query(Account).with_for_update().get(second)
        source, target = (a, b) if a.id == from_id else (b, a)

        if source.currency != target.currency:
            raise CurrencyMismatch(source.currency, target.currency)
        if source.balance < amount:
            raise InsufficientFunds(from_id, amount, source.balance)

        source.balance -= amount
        target.balance += amount
        session.add(Transfer(key=idempotency_key, src=from_id, dst=to_id,
                             amount=amount, at=utcnow()))
    return {"status": "ok"}

The second version isn't harder to generate than the first, and this is the point rather than an objection to it. Any competent model will produce something close to it when the request says so: serialise the transaction, lock in a fixed order, require an idempotency key, reject non-positive amounts, check the currencies, and write an audit row.

The scarce input isn't the ability to write those lines. It's knowing that each of them has to exist, which is knowledge acquired by having watched the first version fail, and which the person writing the prompt either has or doesn't have.

The code became cheap, but the list did not. The complete version, with the exception hierarchy, the retry envelope, the double-entry ledger, and the nine tests that separate it from the first, is reproduced in Appendix D.1. It runs to roughly three hundred lines against the ten that express the requirement.

This is the mechanism by which producing more code fails to translate into producing more value, and it's not a subtle or contested mechanism. It's simply that code is an intermediate good in a production process whose other inputs are scarce. And increasing the supply of an intermediate good doesn't increase output when a different input is binding.

The remainder of this section examines the evidence that this is precisely what has occurred.

3. The Production Funnel: What Happened When 100,000 Developers Received Agents

The most direct large-scale evidence on this question comes from a 2026 study published by the National Bureau of Economic Research, which examined more than one hundred thousand GitHub developers across successive generations of AI coding tools.

The research design exploits the fact that these tools arrived in distinct waves: first autocomplete, then interactive coding agents operating in a conversational loop, then autonomous agents capable of executing multi-step tasks with limited supervision. And this allowed the authors of the study to observe how developer behaviour changed as capability increased.

The effect on code production was unambiguous and large. Autocomplete increased coding activity by approximately 40 percent. Interactive coding agents increased it by approximately 140 percent. Autonomous agents increased it by approximately 180 percent.

These aren't marginal improvements: a near-tripling of commit volume across a population of 100,000 developers represents one of the largest measured productivity shifts in the history of the software industry. Anyone who doubts that AI does something real to the mechanics of programming should sit with that number before proceeding.

Across more than 100,000 developers, autocomplete increased coding activity by approximately 40 percent, interactive coding agents by approximately 140 percent, and autonomous agents by approximately 180 percent. (National Bureau of Economic Research)

What happened next is the finding that matters. The 180 percent increase in commits translated into only about 50 percent more projects and approximately 30 percent more actual releases. Across four major application marketplaces, the researchers observed a moderate increase in the number of new applications published but no corresponding increase in total usage.

The funnel, in other words, narrowed sharply at every stage after generation, and by the time the additional output reached the point at which economic value is actually realised (a customer using the software), the measured effect had disappeared entirely.

The arithmetic is worth stating explicitly because it's easy to lose in the percentages. If commits rise by 180 percent and releases rise by 30 percent, then the ratio of commits to releases has increased by a factor of roughly two and a sixth: each release now consumes substantially more generated code than it did before.

# The NBER funnel stated as arithmetic rather than as percentages, with
# every stage indexed to its own pre-agent baseline of 1.00.
stage_multiple = {
    "commits":  2.80,   # +180 percent
    "projects": 1.50,   # +50 percent
    "releases": 1.30,   # +30 percent
    "usage":    1.00,   # no measured change
}

previous = 1.00
for stage, multiple in stage_multiple.items():
    print(f"{stage:>9}  {multiple:.2f}x   "
          f"passed through: {multiple / previous:.0%}")
    previous = multiple

#   commits  2.80x   passed through: 280%
#  projects  1.50x   passed through: 54%
#  releases  1.30x   passed through: 87%
#     usage  1.00x   passed through: 77%
#
# Generated artefacts consumed per shipped release, against the baseline:
#   2.80 / 1.30 = 2.15x

The column on the right is the one that carries the argument. Each figure is the proportion of the preceding stage's gain that survived into the next, and the conversion is worst at the first transition after generation. That's the throat of the funnel, and it's where the inputs that weren't expanded by the tools (review capacity, requirement clarity, integration effort, and the attention of people who understand the system) do their binding.

Before that ratio can carry any argumentative weight, one measurement question has to be answered, and this report can't fully answer it. A commit is a unit of developer behaviour, not a unit of code, and the tools under study changed the behaviour directly: an agent working through a task in steps produces a commit per step, where a person working through the same task by hand might have produced one at the end.

Some unrecoverable fraction of the 180 percent is therefore an artifact of the instrument rather than a change in what was built, and the size of that fraction determines how much of the attenuation is real.

A study reporting lines changed, or the distribution of commit sizes before and after adoption, would resolve it. Until one does, the true reading is that the direction of the funnel is well established (the ratio of generated artifacts to shipped releases rose, and rose substantially) while the specific factor of two and a sixth should be treated as an upper bound on the true attenuation rather than a measurement of it.

The final stage of the funnel requires a separate explanation, and conflating it with the others would be an error that this report has no interest in committing.

That new applications appeared in marketplaces without total usage rising isn't evidence about engineering capacity at all. Total marketplace usage is bounded by how many people there are and how much attention and money they have, which is a demand-side constraint that no amount of engineering judgment, review capacity, or architectural discipline would relieve.

It's close to definitional that increasing supply into a demand-constrained market doesn't increase aggregate consumption of that market. The usage finding therefore establishes something real and important: that the binding constraint on software adoption was never the supply of software. But it establishes it about customers rather than about engineers, and it shouldn't be counted as support for the thesis of this report.

The stages that do support that thesis are the earlier ones, where generated code failed to convert into completed projects and completed projects failed to convert into releases.

Within those earlier stages, the bottlenecks appeared after generation rather than during it. Requirements still had to be clarified with people who hadn't fully decided what they wanted. Outputs still had to be reviewed by engineers who could evaluate them, and review capacity didn't increase by 180 percent.

Components still had to be integrated with systems that had their own constraints. Products still had to be tested against conditions nobody had specified, secured against adversaries who hadn't been modelled, deployed into environments that behaved differently from staging, supported by people who had to understand them, and, most stubbornly of all, adopted by customers whose attention, budgets, procurement processes, and switching costs were entirely unaffected by the fact that the software had become cheaper to produce.

The study also estimated a substitution elasticity of only 0.25 between AI and human effort. This is a technical parameter with a plain-language meaning: it indicates that AI and human work remain strongly complementary rather than substitutable, and that a company can't straightforwardly trade one for the other at constant output.

An elasticity of that magnitude implies that reducing human input while increasing AI input degrades production substantially, which is a formal statement of the intuition that the two inputs do different things. AI accelerated one part of the production process, and accelerated it dramatically, but the surrounding human system determined how much of that acceleration reached anyone who would pay for it.

The estimated substitution elasticity between AI and human engineering effort was approximately 0.25, indicating strong complementarity rather than straightforward replacement. (National Bureau of Economic Research)

That parameter also creates an obligation this report must discharge in Part III rather than leave hanging, because at first sight it predicts the opposite of what the labour data show. If AI and human effort are strong complements, then making AI abundant and cheap should raise the marginal product of the human input and therefore raise demand for it.

Part III will document falling entry-level hiring and a fifteen-to-one skew toward senior roles, which looks like the signature of substitution rather than complementarity.

The reconciliation is that the estimated elasticity is an aggregate over a workforce that's not homogeneous in this respect, and that it conceals two opposite relationships: the tasks that define junior work are the bounded, well-specified ones on which AI substitutes most readily, while the planning, verification, and accountability that define senior work are the ones with which it composes.

An aggregate elasticity of 0.25 is consistent with a profession in which one half of the workforce is being complemented and the other is being displaced, and that's the reading this report adopts throughout.

The production funnel that emerges from these figures can be stated compactly, and it remains the single most important quantitative expression of the argument in this report, with the qualifications above attached: substantially more generated code produced fewer completed projects than the code volume would suggest, and those projects produced fewer releases still.

The stages between generation and release are the places where human judgment, human coordination, and human attention are the limiting inputs, and none of those inputs was expanded by the arrival of the tools. What happened after release was governed by customer demand, which is a separate constraint and a separate argument.

4. What Generation Actually Costs

The argument to this point has followed the convention of the wider discussion and treated generation as though it were free.

Measured against the wage of a person writing the same code by hand, that convention was defensible when the tools were autocomplete. It's no longer defensible now that the dominant mode is an agent running for minutes or hours against a large context, and the gap between the two framings has grown large enough to change conclusions rather than merely to qualify them.

A report whose title asserts that code is becoming cheaper owes the reader an account of what it actually costs.

The forecast that has focused industry attention came from Gartner in June 2026, which projected that artificial-intelligence coding token costs will meet or exceed the average software engineer's monthly salary by 2028.

The accompanying analysis is explicit that this is a warning about ungoverned consumption rather than a prediction of inevitability, and the analyst's framing is worth quoting because it states the trade-off precisely:

The same analysis puts the productivity contribution of assistive development at up to 20 percent, which is the other half of the ratio and the reason the forecast matters.

Gartner projects that AI coding token costs will meet or exceed the average software engineer's monthly salary by 2028, against a productivity contribution from assistive development of up to 20 percent. (Gartner)

One qualification must travel with that figure wherever it's repeated, and it's routinely dropped. The forecast is anchored on a global average salary of approximately $2,000 per month, which is not a United States crossover point and was never claimed to be. Coverage of the forecast notes that in India the comparison may already hold for an engineer with four to six years of experience, while prevailing salaries in the United States and Western Europe place the crossing considerably further out (CIO).

Read carelessly, the headline says agents will cost more than engineers. Read correctly, it says the ratio of tool cost to labour cost varies by an order of magnitude across the world's engineering labour markets, and that the economics of AI-assisted development are therefore geographically specific in a way the discourse hasn't absorbed.

Published vendor figures give the current level. Enterprise deployments of one widely used coding agent run at approximately $13 per developer per active day and $150 to $250 per developer per month, with ninety percent of users remaining below $30 on any active day (Anthropic).

Heavily automated workflows, in which agents run continuously rather than being invoked, are reported well above that range. Against a fully loaded engineering salary, these aren't yet large numbers. They're also not the rounding error that the phrase "cheap code" implies, and their trajectory is the more interesting quantity.

That trajectory contains a finding which should unsettle anyone assuming the cost problem solves itself. In April 2026 the vendor more than doubled its own published estimate of what an enterprise developer spends, and the reason given was that a more capable frontier model had become the default (Yahoo Finance). A capability improvement raised the cost per developer rather than lowering it.

The mechanism isn't mysterious and is familiar from every previous efficiency gain in computing: when a more capable model arrives, it's not used to perform yesterday's task more cheaply but to attempt harder and longer-running tasks that were previously out of reach. Cost per token falls, while tokens per task rise faster. Anyone forecasting that improving models will make agentic development cheap should first explain why this observation is not the general case.

The demand side confirms the pattern at market scale. Weekly token processing volume on one large routing platform rose from 0.4 trillion in December 2024 to 27.0 trillion by March 2026, an increase of roughly sixty-eight times in fifteen months. Software-engineering agents specifically consume more than a thousand times the tokens of single-turn reasoning, at an input-to-output ratio exceeding 150 to 1 (arXiv).

The input-heavy ratio is the technical signature of agentic work: the model is repeatedly re-reading a large context in order to take one small action, and it's the reason agentic costs bear so little relation to the length of the output produced.

Weekly token volume on a major routing platform rose from 0.4 trillion in December 2024 to 27.0 trillion by March 2026, approximately 68 times in fifteen months, with software-engineering agents consuming over 1,000 times the tokens of single-turn reasoning at an input-to-output ratio above 150 to 1. (arXiv)

The most useful statistic in this literature, however, is not a level or a growth rate but a ratio, and it reproduces the structure of Section 3 in a different currency.

On a standard software-engineering benchmark, one widely studied agent configuration cost approximately $0.24 per instance attempted and approximately $32.50 per issue actually resolved (arXiv). The gap between those two numbers is a factor of roughly one hundred and thirty-five, and it exists for exactly the reason the commit-to-release gap exists: most attempts don't convert.

A buyer looking at the cost of an attempt is looking at the wrong number in the same way that an executive looking at commit volume is looking at the wrong number. The correction in both cases is to divide by the conversion rate rather than to admire the numerator.

# Two ways of pricing the same agent, from the benchmark cost study above.
COST_PER_ATTEMPT  = 0.24     # dollars, per instance the agent is given
COST_PER_RESOLVED = 32.50    # dollars, per issue actually resolved

print(f"implied resolution rate: {COST_PER_ATTEMPT / COST_PER_RESOLVED:.1%}")
# implied resolution rate: 0.7%

# The number an engineering leader actually needs is neither of the above,
# because the expensive input is not the model. It is the person who has to
# read what the model produced before it can be merged.
def cost_per_delivered_change(attempts, unit_cost, merge_rate,
                              review_minutes, reviewer_rate):
    machine = attempts * unit_cost
    merged  = attempts * merge_rate
    human   = merged * (review_minutes / 60) * reviewer_rate
    return (machine + human) / max(merged, 1e-9), machine / (machine + human)

total, model_share = cost_per_delivered_change(
    attempts=1_000, unit_cost=0.24, merge_rate=0.30,
    review_minutes=25, reviewer_rate=95.0)

print(f"${total:,.2f} per merged change; {model_share:.1%} of it is inference")
# $40.38 per merged change; 2.0% of it is inference

The proportions in that calculation are the substance of it rather than the precision. Under assumptions that are unremarkable for an organisation reviewing agent output seriously, the inference bill is two percent of the cost of a delivered change and the review is ninety-eight.

An organisation that halves its token spend has moved one percent of its engineering cost. An organisation that halves the time a competent reviewer needs to reach a confident decision has moved something close to half of it, and that's a tooling, architecture, and testing problem rather than a procurement one.

This has a methodological consequence that the evaluation literature has already drawn. Accuracy measurements that don't control for cost aren't decision-useful, because an agent can be made to look better simply by being allowed to spend more.

When the comparison is made properly, simple baseline configurations turn out to dominate elaborate state-of-the-art agents on some coding benchmarks at approximately fifty times lower cost (arXiv). The recommendation that follows (report the accuracy-cost frontier rather than a leaderboard position) is the same discipline this report argues for on the delivery side in Section 44, arrived at independently by researchers looking at a different problem.

On a coding benchmark, simple baseline agent configurations Pareto-dominated complex state-of-the-art agents at approximately 50 times lower cost, indicating that accuracy figures uncontrolled for cost are not decision-useful. (arXiv)

There's also now a benchmark denominated in the market price of the human labour it replaces, which is the cleanest available framing of the question this section asks. It comprises over 1,400 real freelance software engineering tasks carrying $1,000,000 in actual payouts, ranging from $50 bug fixes to $32,000 feature implementations, and it scores a model by the dollar value of the work it completes rather than by a percentage. Frontier models at the time of publication earned something over $400,000 of the million available (arXiv).

That result can be read in either direction, which is precisely why it's worth citing: a machine capturing forty percent of the market value of a real freelance software market is a remarkable capability result, and a machine leaving sixty percent of it uncaptured is a measurement of how much of commercially valuable engineering remains outside its reach.

A benchmark of over 1,400 real freelance tasks carrying $1,000,000 in actual payouts, ranging from $50 bug fixes to $32,000 feature implementations, saw frontier models earn somewhat over $400,000 of the total available. (arXiv)

Two conclusions follow, and the second matters more than the first.

The first is terminological: this report will continue to say that code has become cheaper, because measured against the wage bill of writing it by hand it plainly has.

But you should understand the claim as one about a ratio rather than about an absolute approaching zero. You should also understand that the ratio is deteriorating for agentic workloads even as the price per token falls.

The second is that this evidence strengthens rather than weakens the argument of the report. If generation were genuinely free, then generating speculatively and discarding what fails would be a rational strategy and judgment about what to build would matter less.

Because generation carries a real and rising marginal cost, and because the cost per delivered outcome exceeds the cost per attempt by two orders of magnitude, the decision about what to attempt reacquires economic weight.

Cheap-but-not-free generation makes the scarce input (knowing what's worth generating and being able to tell whether the result is correct) more valuable, not less.

A caution belongs here rather than in the appendix. Prices in this market are volatile, competitive, and possibly subsidised by capital seeking market share. Don't read anything in this section as a forecast of what inference will cost in three years.

The direction of the per-token price is downward and has been steeply so. The direction of the per-task cost has been upward, because task ambition has grown faster than unit price has fallen. Which of those dominates in any particular organisation is an empirical question about that organisation's workload. The practical recommendation is simply that engineering leaders should measure their cost per delivered change rather than assuming it's negligible, because at present most can't state it.

5. The Case for AI: What the Positive Evidence Actually Shows

It would be straightforward, and dishonest, to build the argument of this report exclusively from studies showing disappointing aggregate outcomes.

The experimental literature also contains findings of substantial, well-measured, statistically robust gains, and these deserve to be presented at full strength rather than acknowledged in passing. They define the conditions under which AI assistance genuinely does what its advocates claim.

The clearest of these comes from a randomised controlled experiment involving ninety-five professional developers, all of whom were asked to build the same JavaScript HTTP server.

Developers with access to GitHub Copilot completed the task in an average of one hour and eleven minutes, compared with two hours and forty-one minutes for the control group. This is an improvement in task completion speed of 55.8 percent, with a 95 percent confidence interval running from 21 percent to 89 percent. Completion rates also improved, with 78 percent of the treatment group finishing the task against 70 percent of the control group (Microsoft).

In a randomised controlled experiment with 95 professional developers building the same JavaScript HTTP server, GitHub Copilot increased task completion speed by 55.8 percent, reducing average completion time from 2 hours 41 minutes to 1 hour 11 minutes, with completion rates of 78 percent versus 70 percent. (Microsoft)

That is a large effect on a clean experimental design, and it shouldn't be explained away. The characteristics of the task, though, are as informative as the result: the problem was bounded, the specification was clear, the scope was fixed, the codebase was new, there was no existing architecture to respect, no production system to avoid destabilising, no team convention to conform to, no historical decision to understand, and no maintenance horizon over which the choices made would have to be lived with.

These are precisely the conditions under which generation is the dominant cost, and under such conditions the evidence indicates that AI assistance roughly halves the time required.

A second study, examining code quality rather than speed, found improvements as well. Among two hundred and two developers with at least five years of professional experience, those using Copilot were 53.2 percent more likely to pass all ten unit tests associated with the assigned task. Their code showed measured improvements of 3.62 percent in readability, 2.94 percent in reliability, 2.47 percent in maintainability, and 4.16 percent in conciseness, and was approximately 5 percent more likely to receive approval in code review (The GitHub Blog).

The magnitudes on the quality dimensions are modest (low single-digit percentages) but their direction is consistently positive, which contradicts the simplest version of the claim that AI-generated code is uniformly worse.

The unit-test result is considerably larger and suggests that on well-specified problems with clear success criteria, assistance meaningfully improves the probability of arriving at a correct answer.

GitHub has separately reported that Copilot generated approximately 46 percent of the code in files where it was enabled (The GitHub Blog). That figure is a measure of penetration rather than of value, and it should be read carefully: a tool that writes half the characters isn't necessarily doing half the work, since the distribution of difficulty across characters is extremely uneven. But it does establish that the technology has moved well past the stage of novelty and into the ordinary substrate of daily practice.

The adoption picture is confirmed at population scale by Google's DORA research program, which found that approximately 90 percent of technology professionals now use AI at work and that more than 80 percent believe it has increased their productivity (Dora).

The adoption figure and the belief figure are evidence of very different quality, and this report separates them rather than presenting the pair as a single result. Ninety percent adoption is a behavioural measurement and it's close to decisive: a tool that nine in ten devs choose to keep using is delivering something they value, whatever the measured effect on throughput turns out to be.

The eighty percent belief is a self-report, and Section 7 will show experimentally that self-reports of exactly this kind were wrong about the direction of the effect, not merely its size, in the population best placed to judge.

Nothing in this report's argument rests on the belief figure, and it's cited here to describe the profession's experience rather than to establish that the experience was accurate.

The synthesis of the positive and negative evidence isn't that one body of research is right and the other wrong, but that the two are measuring different things.

The Copilot experiments measure bounded, short-horizon, greenfield tasks where generation dominates cost. The NBER study measures the flow of value through an entire production system over time. Both results can be true simultaneously, and the fact that they're both true is the most important structural finding available: AI reliably compresses the generation step, and the generation step is a smaller fraction of total cost in serious engineering than it appears from the outside.

The correct conclusion is therefore task-dependent productivity, not the universal claim that AI always accelerates or the equally unsupportable claim that it always impedes.

6. Borrowing Against Tomorrow: the Maintainability Cost

If the NBER study establishes that generated code encounters bottlenecks on its way to the customer, a second body of research establishes something more uncomfortable: that the acceleration itself can be partly financed by a deterioration in the asset being built.

Researchers at Carnegie Mellon compared 806 open-source projects that adopted Cursor against a matched control group of projects that didn't, tracking their behaviour before and after adoption. The initial effect was dramatic, and consistent with everything the vendor community has claimed. Lines added increased by an average of 281 percent in the first month following adoption and by 48 percent in the second. (CMU School of Computer Science)

Across 806 open-source projects that adopted Cursor, lines added increased by an average of 281 percent in the first month and 48 percent in the second, but the projects accumulated more complexity and code-quality warnings, contributing to lower future development velocity. (CMU School of Computer Science)
